title: Seoul Itinerary for First-Timers: A 5-Day (and 7-Day) Plan
html:
Trying to plan your first trip to Seoul can feel overwhelming — there's a lot to see, and it's hard to know how many days is "enough." This guide gives you a 5-day core itinerary that covers Seoul's must-see highlights at a relaxed pace, plus two extra days you can add on if you have a full week. Every day is built around subway stations, so you won't need a car or a guide to follow along.

Before you start: pick up a T-money card (a rechargeable card sold at any convenience store or subway station) on day one — it works on every subway, bus, and most taxis, and saves you from buying a paper ticket every single ride. Also, download a map app that actually works in Korea, like Naver Map or KakaoMap — Google Maps' walking and transit directions are unreliable here.

Day 1: Gyeongbokgung Palace & Bukchon Hanok Village

Start with Seoul's biggest and most famous palace, Gyeongbokgung (Gyeongbokgung Station, Line 3, Exit 5). It was the main royal palace of the Joseon Dynasty, the kingdom that ruled Korea for about 500 years. Admission is a very cheap ₩3,000 for adults, and it's completely free if you rent a hanbok (traditional Korean clothing) from one of the many rental shops nearby and wear it inside — a fun photo opportunity plenty of tourists do for exactly this reason. Try to catch the Changing of the Guard ceremony at the main gate, which runs a few times a day. One thing to note: the palace is closed every Tuesday, so don't plan this day if yours falls on one. If you happen to be visiting in late September or early October 2026, check for the seasonal night opening (evenings, closed Mondays and Tuesdays) — seeing the palace lit up after dark with far fewer crowds is worth the small extra planning.

Geunjeongjeon, the main throne hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace. Photo: Hhk1201, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Right behind the palace is Bukchon Hanok Village, a hillside neighborhood of traditional wooden hanok houses that people still actually live in. Walk quietly and keep your voice down here — it's a residential area, not a museum, and signs asking for quiet are meant seriously. Finish the afternoon browsing Insadong, a street packed with tea houses, art galleries, and souvenir shops selling traditional crafts.

A quiet street of hanok houses in Bukchon Hanok Village. Photo: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Day 2: Myeongdong, N Seoul Tower & Namsan

Myeongdong (Myeongdong Station, Line 4, Exit 6) is Seoul's busiest shopping street — packed with beauty stores, clothing shops, and street food stalls. Spend the morning browsing, then walk (or take a short taxi) up toward Namsan, the mountain in the middle of the city. You can ride the cable car up, or hike a gentle trail if you'd rather save the fare. At the top sits N Seoul Tower, Seoul's iconic observation tower, where you can see the whole city spread out below — it's especially pretty around sunset. One practical note: as of late 2024, foreign visitors can no longer buy N Seoul Tower observatory tickets online in advance — you'll need to buy them in person at the tower, so budget a little extra time for the ticket line.

N Seoul Tower, seen from Namsan Park below. Photo: travel oriented, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Couples (and plenty of friend groups) also come here to clip a padlock onto the tower's fences as a symbol of their visit — you can buy one from a nearby stall if you want to join in.

Day 3: Hongdae & the Han River

Hongdae (Hongik University Station, Line 2, Exit 9) is Seoul's university and youth culture neighborhood — full of street performers on weekend evenings, indie shops, and affordable cafes. It has a very different energy from the palaces and historic streets you saw earlier in the trip. In the afternoon, head down to Yeouido Hangang Park, one of several large parks along the Han River (Seoul's main river), reachable by subway (Yeouinaru Station, Line 5, Exit 2 or 3). Rent a bike, sit on the grass, or order chicken and beer for delivery straight to your picnic spot — a very popular local pastime that even has its own nickname, chimaek.

Yeouido Hangang Park, one of the most popular Han River parks in Seoul. Photo: Brit in Seoul, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Day 4: Day Trip to the DMZ

The DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is the heavily guarded buffer strip along the border between South and North Korea, about an hour from Seoul. Half- and full-day tours typically stop at sites like the Third Infiltration Tunnel and Imjingak Park, and are one of the most popular day trips for first-time visitors. Two important things to know: you must book through a licensed tour company, and you need to book at least 3–7 days in advance so the operator can register your passport details for security clearance — this isn't a same-day or walk-up trip. Bring your actual passport (not a photo of it) on the day. Note that public tours into the Joint Security Area (JSA) at Panmunjom itself have been suspended since 2023, so standard DMZ tours focus on the tunnel, observatory, and Imjingak area instead. If the DMZ doesn't interest you, a relaxed day trip to Nami Island (a small tree-lined island reached by ferry, about 1.5 hours from Seoul) is a popular, easier-to-book nature alternative.

Freedom Bridge at Imjingak, one of the stops on many DMZ day tours. Photo: Lance Vanlewen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Day 5: Dongdaemun Design Plaza & Last-Minute Shopping

Wind down (or wrap up, if you're only doing 5 days) at Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) (Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station, Lines 2/4/5, Exit 1), a striking curved building designed by architect Zaha Hadid that hosts exhibitions and design events. Around it, the Dongdaemun shopping district comes alive at night, with malls that stay open into the early morning — a good last stop for souvenir shopping if you're leaving the next day. If you have time, use your last afternoon to double back to anything you missed, or to visit a jjimjilbang (Korean bathhouse and sauna) for a relaxing, very local way to spend a few hours.

Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) at night. Photo: Eugene Lim, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Have a Full Week? Day 6: Everland Theme Park

If you're staying seven days, use one of your extra days for Everland, Korea's largest theme park, in Yongin (about an hour outside Seoul, reachable by shuttle bus or the Everline light rail plus a connecting bus). Foreign passport holders can usually buy a discounted "foreigner-only" day pass through booking platforms like Klook or KKday — it's well worth comparing prices there before buying at the gate. The park mixes rollercoasters with a safari zone and, depending on the season, flower festivals or light displays. If theme parks aren't your thing, swap this day for Suwon Hwaseong Fortress instead — a UNESCO World Heritage 18th-century fortress wall you can walk along, easily reached by subway (Line 1) plus a short bus or taxi ride.

Everland, Korea's largest theme park, in Yongin. Photo: Craig Nagy, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Day 7: Insadong Revisit, Ikseondong & Final Souvenirs

Spend your last full day somewhere slower-paced. Ikseondong, a small hanok neighborhood a short walk from Insadong (Jongno 3(sam)-ga Station, Line 1/3/5, Exit 4), has been converted into a maze of trendy cafes, dessert shops, and bars tucked inside century-old traditional houses — a nice contrast to Bukchon's quieter residential feel on Day 1. It's also an easy afternoon to finish any souvenir shopping list, since Insadong and Ikseondong sit right next to each other. Pack an extra tote bag; you'll probably need it by now.

Insadong Street, right next to the Ikseondong hanok cafe district. Photo: Choi2451, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Locals Actually Do

Most Seoul residents don't try to see one "big" attraction every single day — a packed schedule like this is really a tourist pace. Locals visiting these same neighborhoods on a day off usually pick just one area and linger: one palace or one park, then a long, unhurried cafe stop nearby. If you're feeling rushed by Day 4 or 5, it's completely fine to drop a stop and slow down — nothing on this list will be your only chance to see Seoul again.

5-Day vs. 7-Day Itinerary: Which Should You Pick?

PlanCoversPaceBest for
5 daysPalaces & hanok villages, Myeongdong & N Seoul Tower, Hongdae & Han River, one DMZ or Nami Island day trip, DongdaemunFairly packed, one main stop per dayA first visit with limited vacation time
7 daysEverything above, plus Everland (or Suwon Hwaseong Fortress) and a slower final day around Insadong/IkseondongMore relaxed, room to skip or swap a dayFirst-timers who also want a theme park day or extra buffer for jet lag

💬 Building your own Seoul itinerary? Tell us your travel dates and interests in the comments — happy to help you fit these days together!
meta_description: A beginner-friendly 5-day Seoul itinerary for first-timers, plus 2 extra days for a week: palaces, N Seoul Tower, Hongdae, the DMZ, and Everland, all by subway.
